title: Peer snapshot synchronization
one: When a new participant joins a room, peers can answer a snapshot request with their current shared coordination records so the newcomer does not need a central application database.
steps: Join with a non-sensitive room ID.
Let snapshot exchange complete before editing shared records.
Review received projects/tasks/decisions/comments.
Resolve conflicts using revision and update timestamps.
Export a local JSON backup before major merges.
advanced: This build uses a Trystero request action for state snapshots. Every peer can respond with a sanitized, bounded snapshot. Received records pass the same schema whitelist used by file imports.
expert: Snapshot sync is eventual, peer-provided state—not consensus. For stronger consistency, add signed operation logs, vector/Lamport clocks, CRDTs or an authoritative service appropriate to the governance requirements.

title: TURN as explicit fallback
one: WebRTC usually connects peers directly, but some NAT/firewall combinations require TURN. TURN relays packets when direct connectivity cannot be established.
steps: Try direct connection first.
If SDP is exchanged but peers never connect, review Trystero join errors.
Add a TURN URL and short-lived credentials only when needed.
Test across real institutional networks.
Monitor relay cost and retention/logging policy.
advanced: Trystero accepts turnConfig while retaining its default STUN servers. TURN is transport fallback, not hidden application storage; peer traffic remains WebRTC encrypted, but a relay still observes transport metadata.
expert: Use time-limited TURN credentials, TLS where supported, capacity planning, abuse controls and regional failover. Treat TURN operator access and network metadata as part of the threat model.

title: Public Commons and unverified presence
one: The default public room is a rendezvous for collaboration presence. A Trystero peer ID proves only that a browser peer is connected; it does not verify a person's name, employer or authority.
steps: Do not trust role labels as identity proof.
Share no protected records in the public room.
Use a password-protected private room for working groups.
Verify organizational identity out-of-band for consequential decisions.
Record authoritative decisions in your formal system of record.
advanced: Pseudonymous presence can support discovery and lightweight collaboration, but identity assurance is a separate system. Room passwords strengthen session-description encryption and access by shared secret; they do not establish institutional identity.
expert: For higher assurance, add an explicit admission handshake with signed organizational keys, short-lived credentials or an institution-managed identity layer while preserving data-minimization principles.

title: Texas broadband project pipeline
one: Texas now has overlapping broadband programs at different stages. Treat award, construction, activation and adoption as separate states.
steps: Start with BDO BEAD/BOOT award files.
Locate the project/location identifier.
Check the latest completion status or grant agreement.
Compare FCC-map claims with local evidence.
Record activation only after service is actually orderable/confirmed.
advanced: BEAD, BOOT, pole replacement, middle-mile, local utility work and private construction can interact. A project registry should record program, awardee, geography, technology, stage, dependencies, challenge history and freshness date.
expert: For longitudinal analysis, version the underlying FCC Fabric/location set and preserve award amendments. Avoid comparing location counts across Fabric versions without documenting the change in the denominator.

title: Institution-to-family collaboration design
one: Cross-domain work succeeds when every participant knows what they contribute, what they need from others, and what constitutes an accepted handoff.
steps: Name the shared outcome.
List families, businesses, institutions, operators and government roles.
Define inputs/outputs for each role.
Create tasks, open questions and handoffs.
Record decisions with evidence and review triggers.
advanced: Use the project record as a boundary object. Keep discipline-specific detail in its native language, but normalize interface fields: owner, input, output, units, deadline, evidence, uncertainty and acceptance condition.
expert: Model the collaboration as a typed dependency graph. Separate governance authority, technical responsibility, funding responsibility, operations responsibility and affected-party voice; they are often held by different actors.

title: Data sovereignty and conflict resolution
one: Local-first means your browser holds the working record by default. Sharing is explicit, backups are portable, and no automatic cloud account is required for core functions.
steps: Export JSON backups regularly.
Keep sensitive records out of peer rooms.
Review imported schema before merge.
Use revisions/timestamps to resolve ordinary conflicts.
Preserve authoritative external records in their official systems.
advanced: This build whitelists fields, limits imported file size and sanitizes peer records. Local-first is not the same as infallible persistence—browser storage can be cleared or evicted.
expert: For institutional deployment add retention policies, encrypted-at-rest storage where justified, signed exports, migration tests, access-control boundaries and a documented conflict-resolution authority.

title: Actionable Cross-Domain Nexus
one: Turn a shared outcome into explicit system dependencies, baseline tasks and interface handoffs that can be saved into the coordination board.
steps: Write one measurable outcome.
Select at least two systems that can enable or block it.
Generate the dependency plan.
Review owner, evidence, threshold and acceptance condition for each interface.
Save the plan as executable tasks and handoffs.
advanced: Treat each cross-domain edge as an interface contract rather than a vague relationship.
expert: Use typed dependency edges, boundary objects, versioned assumptions and explicit authority/resource metadata for complex portfolios.

title: Cascade Lab to action conversion
one: The Cascade Lab exposes a planning heuristic, then turns its output into prioritized actions, evidence questions, handoffs and optional quests.
steps: Enter the stressors you want to explore.
Set duration and readiness.
Inspect propagated scores and the disclosed method.
Review generated actions and evidence questions.
Convert to project work only after local validation.
advanced: The model propagates user-entered stress through a fixed dependency graph and does not calculate event probability.
expert: Replace heuristic weights only with locally validated dependency matrices, service thresholds or calibrated models, while preserving assumptions and version history.
